title: Inside the lines
hook: National averages hide big differences between a country's own regions.
notes: Austria and Germany: Eurostat regional accounts (GDP per inhabitant, current euros, 2024), population on 1 January 2025, country of birth from the 2021 census (NUTS 2 for Austria = Bundesländer, NUTS 1 for Germany = Länder). United States: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 1-year, median household income. India: population from the 2011 census (latest full count), re-cut to today's states and union territories; GDP per person from Kummu et al. (2025), based on Reserve Bank of India state accounts scaled to national purchasing-power figures — compare states with each other rather than reading absolute levels. Region outlines: Natural Earth.

scenes.title: Austria, Land by Land
scenes.text: In Austria, output per person is highest in Salzburg (about €65,800 in 2024) and Vienna (€61,900), and lowest in Burgenland (€39,000). Vienna also stands out for how international it is: 37% of its residents were born abroad, against 20% for Austria as a whole.

scenes.title: Germany's east–west gap
scenes.text: Thirty-five years after reunification, the five eastern Länder still produce less per person than any western one: around €37,000–40,000 against €43,000–60,000 in most of the west. Hamburg, a port and business city, leads at €87,500.

scenes.title: American incomes
scenes.text: The typical household in Washington, D.C., Massachusetts or New Jersey earns over $100,000 a year. In Mississippi it is about $59,000, the lowest of any state.

scenes.title: India's states are countries
scenes.text: Uttar Pradesh alone had about 200 million people at the last census, as many as Brazil. Income gaps are wide too: output per person in Goa is roughly ten times that of Bihar, India's poorest state.
